extracted.intended_audience: creative writers, literature students, and general readers interested in narrative theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and conceptual criteria for creating and understanding antagonists in fiction, including types (person, force, trait), their narrative function, and design principles for effective opposition to the protagonist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antagonist definition
rubrics_metrics.description: An antagonist is a character in a story who is presented as the main enemy or rival of the protagonist and is often depicted as a villain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core definitional criterion: the antagonist stands in opposition to the protagonist. Note the phrasing 'often depicted as a villain' acknowledges exceptions; the definition centers on the role (opposition) rather than moral label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antagonist vs. villain (heroes and villains)
rubrics_metrics.description: While narratives often portray the protagonist as a hero and the antagonist as a villain, the antagonist does not always appear as the villain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page gives counterexamples (e.g., Harry Potter and Lord Voldemort vs. Light Yagami and L in Death Note where protagonist is a villain and antagonist an opposing hero). It also notes that antagonists are 'conventionally presented as making moral choices less savory than those of protagonists' but that this is only a convention — moral alignment is not required. Example: Macduff in Macbeth may be morally correct despite opposing the protagonist. TV examples (J.R. Ewing, Alexis Colby) show antagonists can become breakout, sympathetic characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antagonists can be non-evil or unlikeable characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters may be antagonists without being evil – they may simply be injudicious and unlikeable for the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that in some stories (e.g., The Catcher in the Rye) almost every character other than the protagonist may function as an antagonist. Javert (Les Misérables) is given as an example: he displays no malicious intent but represents rigid application of law, creating moral/ethical conflict. This criterion highlights that antagonism can arise from personality, temperament, or role rather than malice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist-as-source (aspects of the protagonist as antagonist)
rubrics_metrics.description: An aspect or trait of the protagonist may be considered an antagonist, such as morality or indecisiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This covers internal antagonists and links to the concept of the antihero: a protagonist's internal traits or conflicts can function as the opposing force that creates obstacles to their goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-personal antagonists (forces, environment, rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: An antagonist is not always a person or people; it can be a force (tidal wave, storm), environmental conditions, societal norms, or rules that cause problems for the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page emphasizes that non-human antagonists 'may or may not create obstacles' in the same way a person does, and explicitly lists natural disasters and societal norms as examples. This criterion encourages writers to consider setting, systems, and impersonal forces as sources of conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative function / usage as plot device
rubrics_metrics.description: An antagonist is used as a plot device to set up conflicts, obstacles, or challenges for the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance clarifies that while not every story requires an antagonist, antagonists often increase drama — in tragedies they often cause the protagonist's main problem or lead groups against the protagonist; in comedies they typically involve the protagonist in comedic situations. This criterion focuses on functional role in plot construction and genre-specific usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antagonist-design technique (John Truby)
rubrics_metrics.description: A true opponent not only wants to prevent the hero from achieving his desire but is competing with the hero for the same goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: John Truby's design principle: 'It is only by competing for the same goal that the hero and the opponent are forced to come into direct conflict and to do so again and again throughout the story.' Use this to design opponents whose objectives intersect the hero's, producing sustained, meaningful conflict rather than mere obstruction.
